newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn cabinet agrees on new German force for Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Bonn cabinet agrees on new German force for Bosnia.

text.p: The Bonn cabinet gave its final go-ahead on Wednesday for 3,000 troops to join NATO's follow-up peace force in Bosnia, paving the way for Germany to take a full military role alongside Western partners for the first time.

If parliament as expected approves the 18-month deployment, the German force will include 2,000 infantry serving in a Franco-German brigade providing security in south-eastern Bosnia as part of the multinational "Stabilisation Force" or "SFOR".
The mission marks the first time that united Germany will send combat troops to serve on the ground in another country.
It also marks perhaps the final step towards the shedding of post-war West Germany's inhibitions, born of the horrors of Nazi militarism, about sending any forces whatsoever abroad.
Bonn had about 4,000 troops in the multinational IFOR mission which is now expiring.

But fears that they could revive memories of the Nazis' World War Two occupation of Yugoslavia and brutal repression of Serb partisans led Germany to limit their mission to logistical tasks such as bridge building and running a field hospital.
In addition, they were stationed in Croatia rather than Bosnia to avoid any potential confrontations with Serbs.
Now Bonn is confident the troops are accepted by all sides, and that increased public acceptance at home means their deployment can be as "normal" as it is for Germany's allies.

In addition to infantry and armoured vehicle-borne reconnaissance forces, it will maintain a reduced contingent of military engineers and medics and continue to deploy its Tornado reconnaissance and anti-radar aircraft as needed. Another 300 soldiers are available as reinforcements.
Germany will also provide headquarters staff including a two-star general who will serve as Chief of Staff under U.S. General William Crouch, commander of the NATO-led peace forces.
It is all a far cry from the Gulf War in 1991 when Germany paid $5.5 billion rather than send troops to join a U.S.-led multinational force to drive Iraq out of Kuwait.
Bonn's embarrassment then, just months after unification, was the trigger for Chancellor Helmut Kohl gradually to make Germany's military a policy instrument again.

The sending of military medics or logistics experts on several U.N. peacekeeping missions was accompanied by supreme court decisions which created a legal basis for troops to be sent on multinational deployments.
Even the partly pacifist opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have given up most of their objections, much to the satisfaction of Kohl, who is keen to ensure broad cross-party support.

The latest resolution risked incurring the SPD's wrath, however, as they had threatened to boycott the parliamentary approval procedure if they were asked to vote on the deployment on Friday before a vote in the United Nations Security Council.
Government sources said the cabinet hoped that the Council might still pass its resolution by Thursday, removing the need to call parliament back from recess next week.
The environmentalist Greens, split between pragmatists and hardline pacifists, have announced they will not support the government's proposal.

But their own alternative motion accepts the need for German troops to go to Bosnia, albeit with the proviso that NATO should pass control of the mission to the U.N. within a few months and place a stronger emphasis on civilian reconstruction.
